questions.q: Why isn't a developer debug log a substitute for an audit log of agent actions?
options: Debug logs and audit logs are exactly the same thing with different names

A debug log is for the developer chasing a bug today and can be noisy and ephemeral; an audit log must be complete and trustworthy for anyone reconstructing events later, including people who weren't present
Debug logs are illegal to keep
Audit logs are only needed if the agent has no human approval step
questions.explain: A debug log serves an immediate development purpose and can be discarded; an audit log is the durable record a compliance reviewer, a different engineer, or an affected customer might need to rely on much later.

questions.q: What makes an agent audit log entry's tool_use_id useful?
options: It is purely decorative and has no functional purpose
It replaces the need to record the tool's input or output
It ties the log entry back to the exact API exchange, so it can be cross-referenced against raw request/response logs if those are also kept
It must be identical across every log entry for a given agent
questions.explain: Because tool_use_id identifies the specific tool_use/tool_result pair from the real API round trip, including it lets an investigator connect the audit entry to the underlying request and response if deeper detail is needed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say rejected and escalated requests should be logged, not just successful actions?
options: Rejections should never be logged, only approvals
A rejection or escalation is evidence the checkpoint is actually catching something, and a pattern of repeated rejections on one tool signals the tool or prompting needs fixing
Logging rejections is only required for actions under $100
Escalations cannot be logged using the same system as approvals
questions.explain: Logging rejections and escalations shows the safety mechanism is functioning, and repeated rejections on the same tool point to a deeper design problem worth investigating rather than a one-off mistake.

questions.q: What does "append-only" mean for an audit log, and why does it matter?
options: Entries can be freely edited as long as a manager approves the edit
Only the most recent entry is kept; older ones are automatically deleted
Entries are written once and never edited or deleted in place — a correction is added as a new entry referencing the original — which is what makes the log trustworthy as a record of truth
Append-only means entries can only be added by the agent itself, never by a human reviewer
questions.explain: A log that can be silently altered after the fact can't be trusted during an incident review; append-only discipline (write once, correct by appending, never mutate) preserves its value as the record of what actually happened.

questions.q: If an agent's tool call is rejected and it retries five minutes later with different arguments that get approved, what does this lesson imply about logging that sequence?
options: Only the final approved attempt should be logged; the rejection should be discarded
Nothing should be logged until the task fully completes
Both the rejection and the later approved attempt should produce their own audit entries, since each is a distinct decision worth recording
The two attempts should be merged into a single entry with no mention of the rejection
questions.explain: Each decision — the rejection and the later approval — is a separate, consequential event; logging both preserves the real sequence of what happened rather than only showing the eventual outcome.
